roots.name: Copper
roots.description: The most-used metal after iron, and in a C64 it is everywhere the electricity goes and everywhere the heat has to leave. The PCB tracks are 35 um copper foil on 1.6 mm FR-4; the switch-mode transformer is wound with 0.2-0.4 mm enamelled magnet wire; the rectifiers and the regulator leadframes are copper. The edge connector fingers and the heatsink mounts are copper alloy. All of it starts as porphyry ore at 0.4-1% Cu, which is why copper smelters are, in the 1980s, as much sulfuric acid plants as they are metal plants.

facts.label: Ore grade
facts.value: 0.3-1.0% Cu in porphyry; US average fell to ~0.55% by 1980

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.99% (4N) cathode, LME Grade A at 99.9935%

facts.label: Chain
facts.value: ~100 t of 0.6% ore -> 1 t of concentrate at 28% Cu -> ~0.3 t of Cu metal in the concentrate

roots.name: High-purity silicon feedstock (9N polysilicon)
roots.description: The refined element every chip in the machine is cut from. A 1982 Commodore 64 mainboard carried a handful of silicon dies and one quartz crystal, both traceable to this chain: quartzite or silica reduced to 96-99% metallurgical silicon, chlorinated to trichlorosilane, distilled to 9-nines, deposited as polysilicon, then pulled as a single Czochralski crystal. Two corrections to what this node previously said. The board's crystal Y1 is 14.31818 MHz, not 2 MHz; the 2 MHz line is a divided output of the clock circuitry, not a separate crystal, and the 6510 runs at about 1.02 MHz. And the 6510 is an HMOS part (silicon gate, depletion load) so its 1982 die does use a polysilicon gate, not aluminium gate metal. The polysilicon branch below is the route the machine's own chips were made by, not merely the wider industry's.

facts.label: Feedstock purity
facts.value: 9N-11N (99.9999999%) for modern polysilicon; 6N-7N typical of the 1982 era

facts.label: Route
facts.value: trichlorosilane / Siemens

facts.label: Boron budget
facts.value: B must be held near 1 ppb; boron is the contaminant that made metallurgical silicon unusable directly

facts.label: Siemens deposition
facts.value: trichlorosilane reduced by hydrogen on UHF-heated silicon rods held at 1050-1150 C

facts.label: Boron
facts.value: the killer impurity: metallurgical silicon stays unusable until boron is below about 1 ppb

roots.name: Nickel
roots.description: Nickel is small in mass and enormous in function. In a C64 it is the plating on the connector shells and the gold-plated edge connector fingers' underlayer, the constantan and nichrome of the thin-film resistors on the board, the Invar of the composite-video circuit's chroma delay, and the bulk of AISI 304 and 430 stainless in the audio jack and the shield cans. 1982 was the year nickel was in a price crisis. The 1982-83 LME collapse, following the Escondida-adjacent and the Sherritt expansions of the late 1970s, took nickel from about $4/lb in 1980 to under $1.30/lb by 1983.

facts.label: Refined grade
facts.value: 99.8% cathode nickel; 99.9% for plating and for 304 stainless

facts.label: 1982 price context
facts.value: the LME nickel price collapsed from over $4/lb in early 1980 to under $1.50/lb by 1983 - a factor of three in three years

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: sulphide at 1-3% Ni (Sudbury, Thompson, Ranko Inlet) or laterite at 1.5-3% Ni (Cuba, Philippines, New Caledonia, Queensland)

roots.name: Tin
roots.description: Tin is the metal that made electronics solderable. On a 1982 C64 board there are roughly 3,500 through-hole joints and most of them are joined with a lead-tin alloy, so there is a couple of hundred grams of tin per machine. Tin also does two other jobs in the machine: it is the coating on tin-plated steel (tinplate, though a home computer case is not canned food) and it is the facing on tin-plated copper-alloy switch and connector contacts, where it stops the copper from tarnishing and gives a low and stable contact resistance.

facts.label: Refined grade
facts.value: 99.9-99.97% Sn; electrolytic refining reaches 99.97-99.99%

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: cassiterite, SnO2, at 0.2-1.5% Sn in alluvial and lode deposits

roots.name: Lime (CaO) and calcium
roots.description: Lime is one of the most-used industrial chemicals there is, and this tree touches it in four places: the Bayer plant uses it to desilicate and to causticise, the blast furnace uses limestone directly as flux, the PCB fabricator regenerates ferric chloride etchant and neutralises with it, and the metallurgical silicon and tin circuits use lime as a flux and a scavenger. Lime is roasted limestone. Limestone is quarried rock.

facts.label: Kiln temperature
facts.value: 1000-1100 C in a vertical or horizontal lime kiln

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2

facts.label: Loss on ignition
facts.value: ~44% by weight; a 100 t kiln yields roughly 56 t of CaO

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: coke, coal fines or anthracite depending on local availability

facts.label: Slaking
facts.value: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 is exothermic and adds about 65% to the mass

roots.note: Documented: calcination of calcium carbonate in a lime kiln above 900 C gives quicklime, and adding water gives slaked lime. Not established: the 1000-1100 C kiln temperature, the roughly 44% loss on ignition and 56% CaO yield, the 65% mass gain on slaking, and the coke/coal-fines/anthracite fuel list.

roots.name: Cobalt
roots.description: Cobalt is the element nobody thinks of and cannot do without. In a 1982 C64 and its peripherals it is the metal that holds tungsten carbide together in a drill cone, an end mill and a stamping die; the grain-boundary dopant that makes NiZn ferrite behave; the balance element in the iron-nickel-cobalt lid sealed onto a memory chip's ceramic package; a few percent of an Alnico correction magnet; and, at the top of the price range, half of a samarium-cobalt magnet. The mass in any one machine is a few grams. What is worth tracing is where it comes from, because cobalt is almost never mined for itself: it is overwhelmingly a by-product reporting out of somebody else's circuit, most often a copper-cobalt orebody or a nickel refinery, so the cobalt supply chain is largely a set of attachments to the copper and nickel branches.

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: grey-white, hard and brittle, density 8.83 g/cm3, melting point 1495 C

facts.label: Supply character
facts.value: almost entirely a by-product of copper and of nickel; primary cobalt deposits are rare

facts.label: Late-1970s concentration
facts.value: a contemporary industry survey put Zaire at 53% of world output, with Zambia 9%, Australia 7%, New Caledonia 6% and Morocco 6%

facts.label: Price
facts.value: $5.58/lb in 1977, $25/lb in 1980, about $12.50/lb in May 1982, about $5/lb by 1983-84

facts.label: Share of the market
facts.value: superalloys and cemented carbides have historically taken the largest share

roots.note: The market was not short in 1982, which is the opposite of the usual assumption. The genuine disruption was the Shaba invasions of 1977 and 1978 in Zaire, which stopped the Katanga copper mines. The price went from about $5.58/lb in 1977 to about $25/lb in 1980 and then fell back as Zaire's stockpiles came down and nickel-derived supply grew. Even the Shaba shock was milder than expected, because cobalt is a rare metal, its pigment is toxic enough that a formulator could substitute, and the industry had established effective recycling. Which plants contributed how much cobalt in a particular year is not established here.

metal.copper.anode.name: Blister copper anode, 99.9%+
metal.copper.anode.description: Blister is poured into a horizontal straight-mould casting machine. It is a ladle of molten copper that pours into a row of cast-iron moulds on a moving chain, giving a rectangular anode of 200-500 kg, roughly 700-1000 mm long, 400-800 mm wide and 30-50 mm thick, with a hanging loop cast on top. In 1982 the standard anode assay was 99.5-99.9% copper, and the gold and silver in it (typically 5-30 g/t gold equivalent) is why anodes are not made to 99.99%: that would be throwing away money.

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 200-500 kg per anode, 25-50 mm thick

facts.label: Casting method
facts.value: horizontal straight-mould casting machine with a water-cooled chain

metal.copper.block-cave.name: Block cave drawpoints and ore pass
metal.copper.block-cave.description: The block cave is the deepest and most sophisticated piece of 1980s mining engineering anywhere near a C64: a slot is cut along the base of the ore block, the slot is blasted, the overlying ore fractures and subsides into the void, and a finger stoper trains stop releasing ore once the cave front has moved past a drawpoint, to stop surface subsidence from outrunning the cave. Ore falls 100-1000 m to a conveyor at the bottom. Throughput per drawpoint is low (a few hundred tonnes a day) so a big block cave has hundreds of them.

facts.label: Draw height
facts.value: 100-1000 m of vertical ore pass

facts.label: Drawpoint production
facts.value: order 100-800 t/day each

facts.label: Controls
facts.value: finger stopers, or chutes with flow-control doors in modern installations

metal.copper.block-cave.note: Drawpoint rates are mine-specific; medium confidence on the range.

metal.copper.haulage.name: Haul road, the ramp and the truck cycle
metal.copper.haulage.description: The economics of an open pit are a haulage problem. A 130-tonne truck on a 2 km round trip from the loading point to the crusher, at about 25 km/h loaded and 40 km/h empty, takes 3-5 minutes per cycle including spotting and loading, so a shovel with a 4-second loading cycle needs about 6-8 trucks to keep it fed. The ramp grade matters enormously (every 1% of extra grade costs roughly 1-2% of the truck's payload) and so does where the crusher is put. A large porphyry pit moves 100,000-400,000 tonnes a day, and the fleet is 100-400 trucks.

facts.label: Truck
facts.value: 100-150 t payload, 25 km/h loaded

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 3-5 min, so 6-8 trucks per shovel

facts.label: Ramp grade
facts.value: 8-10% typical; every extra 1% costs payload

facts.label: Fleet
facts.value: 100-400 haul trucks at a large porphyry pit

metal.copper.haulage.note: Medium confidence on the cycle times and the grade penalty; both are well documented in mining engineering but vary by operation.

children.name: Suppress the pit dust on the haul road
children.description: A 100,000 t/day pit with unsuppressed haul roads produces a very large tonnage of airborne dust, and by the 1970s that had become a legal problem: the Clean Air Act of 1970 and the 1974 federal mine-safety inspection regime both applied to metal mines, and the pit had to water its roads, restrict the speed on unpaved haulage, and in the worst cases stop blasting in a high wind. So the environment is a genuine node in the middle of the ore chain, not a decoration at the end of it, and it is the same regulation that produced the sinter-plant dust precipitator in the steel branch.

facts.label: Control
facts.value: road watering, speed limits on unpaved haulage, blast restrictions in wind

facts.label: Regime
facts.value: Clean Air Act 1970 and the federal mine-safety inspection regime of 1977

children.note: Medium confidence on the specific US regulatory application to metal mines; the controls themselves are standard.

metal.cobalt.ore.name: Cobalt ore
metal.cobalt.ore.description: Most cobalt never appears as a cobalt mineral at all. In the Copperbelt (the Shaba and Nkana strata of Zaire and Zambia) it sits in the sulphide ores as carrollite, Cu(Co,Ni)2S4, and it is recovered by flotation alongside the copper sulphides, so its output tracks the copper mine's. Where the deposit weathers, the same cobalt is oxidised to heterogenite, CoO(OH), a black manganese-rich oxide in the near-surface ore, and it is the oxide that the later hydrometallurgical flowsheets treat. A third source is asbolane, (Ni,Co)2-xMn4+(O,OH)4.nH2O, the cobalt-nickel-manganese oxide that forms in New Caledonian laterite. Grades are low: laterites run 0.1-1.5% Co, and the oxide zones are mined at a few percent.

facts.label: Copperbelt sulphide
facts.value: carrollite Cu(Co,Ni)2S4, floated with the copper sulphides

facts.label: Oxide zone
facts.value: heterogenite CoO(OH), the near-surface weathering product

facts.label: Laterite
facts.value: asbolane (Ni,Co)2-xMn4+(O,OH)4.nH2O, New Caledonia

facts.label: Grades
facts.value: 0.1-1.5% Co in laterite; the oxide zones are worked at a few percent

metal.cobalt.oxide.name: Cobalt(II) oxide, the additive grade
metal.cobalt.oxide.description: The oxide a component maker actually buys is neither the ore nor the metal but a calcined powder, and in 1982 electronics the grade in question was a few percent of a zinc oxide varistor disc and a trace in a ferrite body. Heating cobalt metal in oxygen gives the blue-black spinel Co3O4, which is the oxide most of the industry actually trades. The green rocksalt CoO underneath it is a different substance with a different stability range, oxidising back to Co3O4 at 600-700 C and reappearing only when the temperature goes above 900 C. That is why the calcining route is described as reducing to the metal by way of Co3O4, and why a supplier's 'cobalt monoxide' and 'cobalt oxide' can be the same powder. The varistor is why this matters. A few percent of cobalt lets a zinc oxide disc hold a wide voltage range without failing, by making the grain boundaries and the grain interiors drift to their breakdown voltages at different rates.

facts.label: The traded oxide
facts.value: blue-black spinel Co3O4, from heating cobalt metal in oxygen

facts.label: The two oxides
facts.value: CoO oxidises to Co3O4 at 600-700 C, and Co3O4 loses oxygen above 900 C to give CoO again

facts.label: Varistor use
facts.value: a few percent in a ZnO disc, to spread the grain-boundary and grain-interior breakdown voltages

metal.cobalt.oxide.note: The CoO/Co3O4 equilibrium is textbook inorganic chemistry. Which specific oxide a 1982 varistor or ferrite supplier used is not established, so the node records the substance rather than a claim about a particular part.

metal.copper.concentrate.name: Copper flotation concentrate (~25-30% Cu)
metal.copper.concentrate.description: A damp, fine, almost black powder shipped by rail or truck to the smelter. What the smelter really wants is not the copper but the sulphur, because that is what makes the smelter a sulfuric acid plant. A 25% Cu concentrate is roughly 50% sulphur and 10% iron, and the smelter's job is to burn out the iron, keep a copper-iron matte, and send every tonne of SO2 to an acid plant.

metal.copper.ore.name: Porphyry copper ore (0.4-1% Cu)
metal.copper.ore.description: A porphyritic intrusion. It is a granite-textured quartz monzonite that has been split by its own crystallisation and had its cracks filled with hot copper-bearing fluids. The copper minerals are chalcopyrite CuFeS2, bornite and chalcocite Cu2S, covellite and enargite Cu3AsS4. The ore body is graded by porphyry systems but the grade is low and getting lower, which is the whole problem with the industry. In 1982 the great producers were Chuquicamata and El Teniente in Chile, Bingham Canyon in Utah, Butte, the Arizona porphyry belt, Oyu Tolgoi and the Escondida development, and the copper belt of northern Zambia.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 0.3-1.0% Cu, 0.3-5% S, 1-5 g/t Au and Ag as by-product credits

facts.label: Main minerals
facts.value: chalcopyrite CuFeS2, chalcocite Cu2S, bornite, covellite, enargite

facts.label: Overburden
facts.value: 50-200 m of barren porphyry and oxidized capping above the sulphide

facts.label: Decline
facts.value: average US head grade fell from ~0.9% in 1960 to ~0.55% by 1980

children.name: Open-pit copper mine
children.description: An enormous terraced pit. Ore is drilled and blasted on 15 m benches, loaded into haul trucks by 3-6 cubic metre shovels or loaded onto a conveyor, and hauled in 100-150 tonne trucks out of the pit on ramps. The waste:ore ratio at a mature porphyry pit is often 2-5:1, which is why the waste dumps are larger than the pit. As the pit deepens into the ore, block caving takes over: a fracture zone is undercut and the ore caves into a series of drawpoints, and the mining cost per tonne collapses. El Teniente in Chile was the world's largest block-cave operation from 1958 onwards.

facts.label: Bench height
facts.value: 12-15 m, blasted

facts.label: Waste:ore
facts.value: 2-5:1 in the mature part of a large porphyry pit

facts.label: Truck capacity
facts.value: 80-150 t; the haul road is often ~1 km round trip per lift

facts.label: Block caving
facts.value: ore broken by a cave above drawpoints, recovered by gravity; production 20,000-100,000 t/day at the largest operations

facts.label: Alternate method
facts.value: long-hole stoping with delayed blasting, used underground when the orebody is steep and deep

metal.nickel.impact-melt.name: Impact melt sheet at the base of the Sudbury crater
metal.nickel.impact-melt.description: A foot-thick to 20 m layer of rock melted and shock-altered by the impact, in which the nickel and copper sulphides were disseminated as droplets. It is a metamorphic and melt rock, not an igneous intrusion, and it is a band about 60 km long and 20 km wide across northern Ontario. The mining is ordinary room-and-pillar or open-pit on a sheet that lies only a few hundred metres below the Huronian cover.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: impact melt and suevite breccia, disseminated Ni-Cu sulphide

metal.silica-sand.name: Industrial silica sand (quartz dune sand)
metal.silica-sand.description: Siliceous sand from a dune or a beach, washed, screened and often magnetically separated to take out the heavy mineral concentrates that would be a nuisance. This is a distinct node from the silicon-grade quartzite: the purity required here is far lower, and this sand is a commodity that the foundry, the glass and the copper industries all pull on. The quartzite that goes into the silicon furnace is a different, much rarer rock.
places: map of the Mississippi valley dune sands

facts.label: Processing
facts.value: wash, screen, dry, magnetite separation; <150 um for foundry and smelter use

facts.label: Vitrified silica
facts.value: used in foundry moulds and in fused silica, at 99.9%+

metal.silica-sand.dune.name: Aeolian dune sand and beach placer
metal.silica-sand.dune.description: Quartz grains rounded by wind or wave, in an unconsolidated surface deposit a few metres to tens of metres thick sitting on older sediment. Dunes along the Mississippi valley, the Great Lakes shorelines and the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the United States were the standard sources, mined with bucket-wheel or dragline dredges. A sand mine is the commonest kind of open pit in the world.

facts.label: Deposit
facts.value: surface dune and beach sand, over bedrock or older sediment

metal.cs2-synthesis.name: Carbon disulphide (CS2)
metal.cs2-synthesis.description: Carbon disulphide, the feedstock for every xanthate collector and for the rayon and cellophane industries, was made in 1982 almost entirely from natural gas or from methane recovered from coke-oven gas: the gas and a fraction of hydrocarbon oil are passed over a silica or alumina gel at 600-700 C, and the carbon disulphide is condensed out. So the flotation collector that separated copper from a porphyry in Nevada was made from gas, and the same molecule went into the rayon that was in the 1980s' idea of a flame-retardant textile. It is a leaf of the copper branch that is unambiguously a chemical plant rather than a mine.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: methane plus naphtha over a silica or alumina gel at 600-700 C

facts.label: Product
facts.value: carbon disulphide, condensed out of the gas stream

metal.cs2-synthesis.note: Medium confidence; the CS2-from-methane route is well documented.

metal.cobalt.ammoniacal-leach.name: Sherritt-Gordon ammonia pressure leach
metal.cobalt.ammoniacal-leach.description: The second big route takes cobalt out of a nickel refinery rather than out of an orebody, and it exists because the nickel circuit was already there. Nickel concentrate or matte is leached with ammonia and ammonium sulphate in horizontal autoclaves under air at elevated pressure, which dissolves the nickel, cobalt and copper as metal-ammine complexes while the sulphide sulphur is oxidised and leaves as ammonium sulphate. It is a saleable fertiliser, which is what made the process pay. Cobalt is then separated from nickel on the fact that the cobalt ammine is far more stable: it is held in solution while the nickel is thrown down, and the cobalt stream is finished separately to metal. Because the feed is somebody else's concentrate, every tonne of cobalt this route makes is a tonne that did not have to be mined.

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: nickel concentrate or matte, and lateritic mixed sulphide precipitate

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: ammonia and ammonium sulphate, air, elevated pressure, horizontal autoclaves

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: the cobalt ammine is much more stable than the nickel ammine, so cobalt is held and nickel is thrown down

facts.label: By-product
facts.value: ammonium sulphate fertiliser, which is what made the process economic

metal.cobalt.ammoniacal-leach.note: The ammonia pressure leach is a mature Sherritt-Gordon process by 1982 and is applied to sulphide concentrate as well as to laterite-derived precipitate. The share of world cobalt it supplied in 1982 is not asserted here.

metal.cobalt.electrolytic.name: Electrolytic refining to 99.8% cathode
metal.cobalt.electrolytic.description: Almost all cobalt metal on the market is won by electrolysis, and that is a deliberate choice about purity rather than about cost. The cobalt hydroxide or the crude metal is dissolved in sulfuric acid to make a cobalt sulphate solution. That solution is fed to an insoluble anode and a cobalt starter cathode, and metal grows on the cathode at a controlled current density while the impurities that are not plating out stay in the bath. The result is a cobalt cathode of about 99.8% (the grade trade calls Falconbridge cathode) and it is the standard feed for the tungsten-carbide industry, because a carbide's cobalt binder has to be fine, uniform and free of the copper, iron and lead that would poison the sintering. Electrolytic cobalt is also how the high-purity metal for superalloys and for the samarium-cobalt magnets was made.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: cobalt sulphate solution, insoluble anode, cobalt starter cathode

facts.label: Product
facts.value: about 99.8% cobalt cathode

facts.label: Other grades
facts.value: about 99.6% from Zambia, 99.3% ingot from the Soviet Union

facts.label: Why the grade matters
facts.value: the WC binder must be fine and free of copper, iron and lead or the carbide will not sinter

metal.cobalt.ore.hydromet.name: Leach the copper-cobalt oxide ore
metal.cobalt.ore.hydromet.description: The oxide ores of the Copperbelt are not smelted for their cobalt: they are leached. The ore is crushed and agitated in a sulfuric acid solution, which dissolves the cobalt and copper as sulphates while the iron stays in the residue as hydroxide, and the pregnant liquor is then taken to a solvent-extraction circuit that pulls the cobalt and copper apart from each other. What comes out of that circuit is a cobalt sulphate solution and, from it, a cobalt hydroxide intermediate that is shipped to a refinery. This is why the cobalt in a 1982 tungsten-carbide drill cone is a chemical-plant product rather than a smelter product, and why the Copperbelt's cobalt followed the fortunes of its acid plants and its export routes.

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: sulfuric acid; cobalt and copper dissolve as sulphates, iron stays in the residue

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: solvent extraction splits cobalt from copper

facts.label: Intermediate
facts.value: cobalt hydroxide concentrate, shipped to a refinery

metal.cobalt.ore.hydromet.note: The sulfate-leach and solvent-extraction flowsheet for Copperbelt oxide ore is well established. Which particular plant or circuit served a given carbide maker in 1982 is not established.

metal.copper.converting.name: Peirce-Smith converter to blister copper
metal.copper.converting.description: The matte from the flash furnace is charged into a horizontal cylindrical steel converter with refractory lining and is blown with air through tuyeres along the side. The iron in the matte oxidises preferentially and goes into a slag that is skimmed off the top every few hours. Once the iron is gone the copper sulphide itself oxidises to copper metal and gives off SO2. The blow takes 4-8 hours and takes 1 t of 60% matte to roughly 0.85 t of blister copper at 98-99% purity, still containing iron, arsenic, antimony and bismuth. The converter is a batch process and by the 1980s it was the target of the new continuous technologies (Noranda, Inductokemco) that were not yet commercial.

facts.label: Converter diameter
facts.value: 3.5-4.8 m, holding 30-120 t of charge

facts.label: Slag
facts.value: iron silicate, skimmed through the converter mouth

metal.copper.converting.note: The Peirce-Smith converter remained the dominant technology into the 2020s, accounting for roughly 90% of world matte refining.

children.name: Fire-refine the blister copper
children.description: Blister copper still carries arsenic, antimony and bismuth, and every one of them is a nightmare for the electrolytic tankhouse because they float to the cathode and destroy the deposit. So the blister is ladle-refined: an oxidising slag of sodium carbonate with the impurities skims off, and then the copper is under-oxidised by dropping in green charcoal to reduce the whole mass back to copper, with the arsenic floatationised out. Where the arsenic is high, the refinery buys a second, smaller furnace.

facts.label: Goal
facts.value: As, Sb and Bi down to 0.02-0.1% before anode casting

facts.label: 1982s practice
facts.value: outright refining in the converter or in a tilting launder furnace; anode casting with a low-As anode became the later route

children.note: There was real variation in refinery strategy between operators in this era; medium confidence on specifics.

children.name: Peirce-Smith converter and its tuyeres
children.description: The converter is a cylindrical steel shell, 3.5-4.8 m inside diameter and 8-10 m long, on trunnions so it can be tilted, lined with magnesite brick, with 20-40 tuyeres along one side at the trunnion line. Air at 30-50% oxygen is blown in at 5-10 bar through water-cooled tuyeres that must be cleared and re-cleared by hand every few hours as the lining erodes, and a tuyeres that is not cleared becomes a plug and the whole heat is lost. The operator tilts the converter so the slag runs out of the mouth, then charges back, and there is no continuous process anywhere else in smelting with quite that much manual involvement. It is the machine that has been unchanged since 1865, and it is still the standard.

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: 3.5-4.8 m diameter, 8-10 m long, on trunnions

facts.label: Tuyeres
facts.value: 20-40, water-cooled, hand-cleaned of lining several times a heat

facts.label: Lining
facts.value: magnesite brick, eroded by the oxidising slag

facts.label: Slag removal
facts.value: the converter is tilted so the slag pours out of the mouth

children.note: Medium confidence; the Peirce-Smith converter geometry is very well documented.

metal.copper.smelting.name: Flash smelting of concentrate to copper matte
metal.copper.smelting.description: Concentrate, silica flux and limestone are dropped into a vertical reverberatory shaft where a hot gas blast, 40-60% oxygen-enriched, burns the concentrate as it falls. Three reactions happen simultaneously: the sulphides oxidise to copper oxide and iron oxide, the oxides react with each other to form a copper-iron matte, and the iron oxide reacts with the silica flux to make a slag. The furnace runs at 1250-1400 C and the products settle into three layers (matte at the bottom, slag above it, and offgas above that) which are tapped separately. By 1982 the flash furnace had largely displaced the reverberatory furnace: it is smaller, faster and needs less fuel, and it works on concentrate straight from the flotation circuit with only a small amount of dried concentrate added as fuel.

facts.label: Dried concentrate as fuel
facts.value: order 0.15-0.35 t per tonne of charge

facts.label: Slag basicity
facts.value: CaO/SiO2 held around 1.0-1.5 so the slag stays fluid

facts.label: SO2 strength
facts.value: 10-14% SO2 in the flash furnace offgas, which the acid plant takes

metal.copper.smelting.note: Copper smelting has barely changed since the 1980s. The industry still runs flash furnaces and Peirce-Smith converters today. The changes since are in slag cleaning and in higher oxygen enrichment.

children.name: Flash furnace, its tuyeres and the concentrate burn
children.description: The furnace is a 20-25 m tall, 5-7 m diameter vertical shaft with a refractory lining, fed by a few hundred tonnes an hour of dried concentrate through a hopper, and blown at the bottom by 30-60% oxygen-enriched air through tuyeres. The concentrate burns as it falls (it is the fuel as well as the charge) so the furnace needs almost no external heat. The reaction happens in the first metre above the tuyeres, the particles are spent, and the matte and slag settle into the two-deep bath at the bottom. The shaft above is used to preheat the charge with the rising offgas, and a flash furnace treats more tonnage in less volume than anything else in smelting.

facts.label: Shaft
facts.value: 20-25 m tall, 5-7 m diameter, refractory lined

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: 200-600 t/h of dried concentrate

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: two layers: matte at the bottom, slag above

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: the concentrate is both the charge and the fuel, so the furnace is close to thermoneutral

metal.copper.tankhouse.name: Electrolytic refining of copper to 99.99%
metal.copper.tankhouse.description: The refinery's tankhouse is a building a couple of hundred metres long containing rows of concrete or rubber-lined steel cells. Each cell holds a 150-250 g/L copper, 200-250 g/L free sulfuric acid solution at 55-65 C, with one or two anodes and one cathode per cell. Current at 20,000-40,000 A per cell is passed through. Copper dissolves off the anode and plates onto the cathode at 98-99% efficiency, and gold, silver, selenium, tellurium and the platinum group fall out as a sludge on the bottom of the cell (the anode slime) which is worth more per tonne than the copper. A refinery producing 100,000 t a year has 300-500 cells and about 100,000 MWh of DC power.

facts.label: Electrolyte
facts.value: 40-60 g/L free Cu2+, 180-230 g/L free H2SO4, 10-25 ppm Fe/As/Bi

facts.label: Current density
facts.value: 10-30 A/m2; 1980s plants commonly 20-25

facts.label: Cell voltage
facts.value: 0.15-0.35 V; power about 200-250 kWh per tonne of copper

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.99% (4N) cathode, LME Grade A 99.9935%, one cathodic plate ~1 m x 1 m, 50-125 kg

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: anode 4-28 days, cathode 4-14 days, by plate weight

metal.copper.tankhouse.note: Tankhouse technology has changed very little since 1982. The later innovation was more automation and the move to higher current density with ion-exchange purification.

children.name: Starter sheets, seeding and the tankhouse floor
children.description: Everything in a tankhouse depends on nucleation. The cathodes start on stainless steel or titanium starter sheets, or on copper seed plates that have been roughened. If too many nuclei start, the deposit is dull and soft and hard to strip; if too few, it is bright and hard and needs a big shear force. The whole art is seeding the right number. The electrolyte is also circulated at 200-400 mm/s across the cell face, because the anode slime would otherwise build up and short.

facts.label: Starters
facts.value: stainless steel or titanium, or roughened copper seed plates

facts.label: Circulation
facts.value: 200-400 mm/s across the cell face

facts.label: Slime removal
facts.value: a travelling scraper on the cell floor

children.note: Medium confidence; the seeding practice is proprietary.

metal.copper.concentrate-handling.name: Thicken, filter and ship the flotation concentrate
metal.copper.concentrate-handling.description: The flotation concentrate at 25-30% Cu arrives as a pulp at 10-20% solids and has to be dewatered to 8-12% moisture to be shipped, because shipping water is shipping money. A 30,000 t/day concentrator produces 1,000-3,000 t of concentrate a day, and it is thickened in a 30-50 m diameter tank, filtered on a vacuum belt or a plate-and-frame press, and often dried to 8% on a steam belt dryer so it does not cake in a railcar. Copper concentrate that arrives wet is worth less per tonne and smelters charge for the water.

facts.label: Moisture in
facts.value: 10-20% solids by weight from the flotation circuit

facts.label: Moisture out
facts.value: 8-12%, or dried to about 8%

facts.label: Dewatering
facts.value: thickener, then vacuum filter or filter press, then a belt dryer

metal.copper.concentrate-handling.note: Medium confidence on the specific flowsheet; the practice is standard.

metal.copper.flotation.name: Froth flotation of chalcopyrite
metal.copper.flotation.description: The slurry is conditioned with lime to a pH of 8-9.5 and with a xanthate collector, then aerated in a bank of 20-50 cubic metre rectangular cells. Air bubbles pick up the particles of chalcopyrite that the collector has made water-repellent and float them into a froth; the gangue stays in the water. Each cell in a bank is stage-controlled, with a froth of 100-300 mm. In 1982 the workhorse collector was sodium or potassium ethyl xanthate, made from carbon disulphide, caustic soda and ethanol, and the frother was pine oil or a synthetic such as methyl isobutyl carbinol.

facts.label: pH
facts.value: 8.0-9.5, set with lime or soda ash

facts.label: Cell size
facts.value: 20-50 m3 rectangular cells, 5-15 in series

facts.label: Concentrate grade
facts.value: 20-30% Cu; about 0.3 t of concentrate per tonne of Cu metal

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 85-92% in a porphyry circuit

facts.label: Collector
facts.value: potassium ethyl xanthate, 5-30 g/t

metal.copper.grinding.name: Crushing and grinding to 100-150 um
metal.copper.grinding.description: The ore arrives at 1 m. It goes through a gyratory crusher, then a semiautogenous mill (which uses the ore itself as the grinding medium, so no steel balls to pay for at that stage), then one or two ball mills in a closed circuit with a spiral classifier and then a cyclone. Autogenous grinding came in during the 1970s and was fully established by 1982 because it both saved the grinding media cost and produced a much cleaner surface. Less steel contamination matters when you are about to float it. Before the mill a 1500-4000 t/h gyratory with a screen at 25-50 mm does the primary crushing, and a 100 g charge goes to the fire assay for total copper while a leach assay of the fines gives the recoverable copper. The difference between the two, the oxide and the locked-up copper, is the number that becomes the contract between the mine and the mill. The grind has to be fine enough to liberate chalcopyrite but not so fine that the froth washes out.

facts.label: Product size
facts.value: P80 of 100-150 um for a porphyry flotation feed

facts.label: Typical circuit
facts.value: one 1.2-1.8 m semiautogenous mill plus two 1-1.2 m ball mills, or SAG plus ball in series

facts.label: Power
facts.value: order 35-55 kWh per tonne of ore ground

facts.label: Steel contamination
facts.value: why autogenous was adopted: iron in the concentrate poisons the smelter

facts.label: Primary crushing
facts.value: 1500-4000 t/h gyratory, screened at 25-50 mm

children.name: Forged steel grinding balls
children.description: Even in an autogenous circuit the ball mills need some steel, and the balls themselves are a ferroalloy product: rail steel or scrap forged and quenched. Hardness matters more than anything. A 1982 ball mill ran 100-150 mm balls in the harder grind, and the wear rate was the plant's second-biggest cost after power. Nickel and chromium in the steel were deliberately kept low here, unlike in a crusher liner.

facts.label: Ball size
facts.value: 100-150 mm for a coarse grind in 1980s practice

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 0.05-0.2 kg of balls per tonne of ore ground

children.note: Consumption depends heavily on the abrasive index of the ore; medium confidence.

metal.nickel.electrowinning.name: Nickel electrowinning from a pure sulphide circuit
metal.nickel.electrowinning.description: Where the ore is sulphide rather than laterite, Sherritt's original ammonia-pressure process dissolves the concentrate in ammoniacal ammonium sulphate at 160-190 F (70-90 C) with oxygen, and then electrowins the nickel directly out of the pregnant liquor onto titanium cathodes in diaphragm cells at a very low voltage, about 0.5-1.0 V, because hydrogen evolution competes and the current efficiency is only 70-85%. This is the Sherritt-Gordon route as it was licensed in 1969-1972, and it is why the company is called after two towns in Manitoba. The cathodes are stripped, briquetted and remelted.

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: ammoniacal ammonium sulphate, 70-90 C, aerated

facts.label: Cathode
facts.value: titanium starter sheets, stripped and briquetted

metal.nickel.electrowinning.note: The 160-190 F optimum is from Sherritt's own published leach chemistry for sulphide concentrates; medium confidence on the current efficiency range.

metal.nickel.mond.name: Mond carbonyl refining (nickel from 99.9 to 99.999)
metal.nickel.mond.description: Ludwig Mond's 1890s process, still used in the 1980s for the last nines. Nickel carbonyl Ni(CO)4 is formed at 50-60 C in a saturator, distilled off as a colourless liquid boiling at 43 C, and decomposed in a decomposer column at 200-230 C onto 99.99% nickel pellets. The trick is that the carbonyl of cobalt is much less volatile and iron forms a non-volatile carbonyl, so the distillation separates the three metals in one operation. It is the same volatility trick as the trichlorosilane column in the silicon branch. Cobalt is recovered from the residue as Co2(CO)8.

facts.label: Carbonyl
facts.value: Ni(CO)4, liquid, boils 43 C at atmospheric pressure

facts.label: Decomposer
facts.value: 200-230 C, produces high-purity nickel pellets

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.99% nickel - the Mondcarbonyl process still supplies the very pure nickel used in plating chemistry

facts.label: Safety
facts.value: extremely toxic; the vapour is the reason Mond refineries had continuous air monitoring from the 1970s

children.name: Why nickel carbonyl is the deadliest room in metals
children.description: Nickel tetracarbonyl is a colourless, volatile liquid that boils at 43 C and is lethal by inhalation at concentrations far below anything that can be smelled. A Mond refinery therefore runs on a rule that no one enters a carbonyl area without a respirator, that the vapour is continuously monitored at the floor and at breathing height, and that the whole plant is vented through a high-temperature incinerator that destroys the carbonyl before releasing it. The 1980s occupational-hygiene literature on nickel carbonyl is a case study in how a process can be kept running at all when the material is that toxic, and the number of fatal poisonings in nickel refineries over the century is a reminder that this is one of the most dangerous processes in the metals industry.

facts.label: Boiling point
facts.value: 43 C at atmospheric pressure

facts.label: Exposure limit
facts.value: of the order of 0.1 ppm as an 8-hour TWA in most jurisdictions by the 1980s

facts.label: Control
facts.value: closed process, continuous air monitoring, and high-temperature incineration of the offgas

children.note: The exposure limit varies by jurisdiction; medium confidence on the specific 1982 figures.

metal.lime.bayer-uses.name: Causticise and desilicate the Bayer liquor
metal.lime.bayer-uses.description: Two unrelated jobs in one plant. Lime added during digestion converts reactive silica (kaolinite) into an insoluble calcium silicate, which would otherwise lock up alumina permanently. This is the single most important reason a high-silica bauxite is unprocessable. Lime also drives the causticisation step, converting the sodium carbonate that accumulates in the Bayer liquor back into caustic, and it helps precipitate iron and titanium as hydroxides. Dosage was order 5-20 kg CaO per tonne of bauxite digested.

facts.label: Dosage
facts.value: order 5-20 kg CaO per tonne of bauxite

facts.label: Desilication reaction
facts.value: kaolinite + lime -> calcium silicate hydrate, permanently wasted

facts.label: Causticisation
facts.value: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3

metal.lime.bayer-uses.note: Dosage range varies with ore; medium confidence.

children.name: Causticise the carbonate back to caustic soda
children.description: The Bayer liquor's sodium carbonate is converted back to caustic with lime: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3, and the calcium carbonate drops out as a filter cake that is a by-product of every tonne of alumina. The cycle is the industry's real control loop, because the caustic that leaves in the red mud is replaced by buying new caustic or by buying lime and causticising it, and the choice is mostly about what lime is available near the refinery. It is also why a bauxite refinery is nearly always built next to a limestone quarry.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3

facts.label: Reactor
facts.value: a stirred causticiser with a settler and a filter

facts.label: Caveat
facts.value: this reaction is reversible; it only goes far enough because the carbonate is continuously removed and the liquor stays dilute

children.note: Medium confidence; the reversibility of the causticisation is the textbook caveat.

children.name: Pre-desilicate the ore by attrition washing
children.description: By 1982 the more elegant answer to high-silica bauxite had arrived and it needs no lime at all: wash the ore. An attrition scrub and a desliming step take out the kaolinite clay before the ore ever meets the caustic, and a gibbsitic ore washed this way can digest without lime at all. The cost of the process is a lot of water and a lot of clay tailings, and the tailings are the same red mud, just produced earlier and with less soda in it. So the industry moved from a chemistry problem to a solids-handling problem, which is a recurring theme in aluminium refining.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: attrition scrub followed by desliming at about 40-60 um

facts.label: Removes
facts.value: typically 1-4% of the mass as clay, which was 10-40% of the reactive silica

facts.label: Trade
facts.value: less lime and less caustic consumed, more water and more tailings

children.note: Medium confidence; the adoption rate was highly ore-dependent.

metal.lime.blast-flux.name: Flux the blast furnace slag with limestone and lime
metal.lime.blast-flux.description: The furnace needs its slag liquid at 1450 C, and calcium is how you get there: CaO absorbs silica into a calcium silicate slag whose liquidus is around 1300-1400 C, so the slag runs off the tuyeres before the iron does. The burden carries roughly 0.25-0.35 t of limestone per tonne of hot metal, deliberately paired with a silica content of about 0.4-0.6 mass units of SiO2 per unit of CaO.

facts.label: Burden rate
facts.value: order 0.25-0.35 t limestone per t hot metal

facts.label: Goal
facts.value: slag basicity CaO/SiO2 of roughly 1.0-1.3

metal.lime.blast-flux.note: Typical burden practice; specific works ran tighter ratios.

metal.lime.kiln.name: Shaft and rotary lime kilns
metal.lime.kiln.description: Limestone plus coke or coal in a vertical shaft 20-40 m tall, or on a rotary kiln, at 1000-1100 C. The vertical kiln (a stack of alternating layers of 250 kg limestone and 40 kg coke in a 2.5-4 m shaft, fired from the bottom) makes the good lime, because the counter-current gas gives a soft, well-calcined product. The rotary kiln makes it faster and is what a captive lime plant at a steelworks or a Bayer refinery used. A 300 t/day shaft kiln is a small plant by industrial standards and there were thousands of them.

facts.label: Shaft kiln
facts.value: 20-40 m tall, 2.5-4 m diameter, 250 kg limestone per 40 kg coke

facts.label: Rotary kiln
facts.value: 1.5-2.5 m diameter, 40-60 m long, inclined, 100-1000 t/day

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: ~110-130 kg coke or coal per tonne of CaO, or ~80 kg in a rotary kiln with a preheater

children.name: Counter-current shaft kiln
children.description: Because limestone goes in at the top at ambient temperature and lime comes out at the bottom at 1000 C, the shaft has to be a heat exchanger as well as a kiln, and that is why a shaft kiln makes a better lime than a rotary one. The gases go up, the stone goes down, and the last of the fuel burns out in the upper third. Below the burn zone the calcination is isothermal, so the lime is not over-heated and does not shrink the kiln's yield.

facts.label: Zones
facts.value: drying, preheating, calcination, burning, cooling

facts.label: Burn zone
facts.value: the upper third of the shaft

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 80-90% of theoretical lime

children.note: Zone layout is standard practice; medium confidence on the yield range.

children.name: Rotary kiln and the preheater
children.description: A 1.5-2.5 m diameter, 40-60 m long rotary kiln, inclined a few degrees, turning 1-3 rpm, heated by a burner at the lower discharge end with coal, coke or gas, and fitted at the upper end with a preheater or a flash dryer for the limestone. The rotary kiln makes worse lime than the shaft kiln (the residence time varies through the bed and the lime is over- and under-burnt) but it makes it faster and it copes with a variable feed, so a captive plant at a steelworks or an alumina refinery used one. A 2000 t/day rotary lime kiln is the sort of thing that sits next to a coke-oven battery.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: 1.5-2.5 m diameter, 40-60 m long, 100-1000 t/day

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: pulverised coal, coke, anthracite or gas, at about 80 kg per tonne of CaO with a preheater

children.note: Medium confidence; the fuel figure assumes a preheater, which is where most of the saving is.

metal.lime.pcb-etch.name: Regenerate ferric chloride etchant with lime
metal.lime.pcb-etch.description: At the board fab the copper etchant is ferric chloride: CuCl2 + FeCl3 -> CuCl + FeCl2, and the ferric is regenerated by blowing air through the spent bath, which is where a great deal of the chlorine chemistry of PCB etching comes from. Lime then raises the pH and drops the copper out as copper hydroxide so the iron can be reclaimed, and lime also neutralises the acid process streams downstream of the etcher. The board's own etch chemistry belongs to the board subsystem; what matters here is that the reagent traces back to a limestone quarry.

facts.label: Regeneration
facts.value: FeCl2 + air/Cl2 -> FeCl3; then CuCl2 + Ca(OH)2 -> Cu(OH)2 + CaCl2

metal.lime.pcb-etch.note: Not established: air-regeneration of the spent ferric-chloride bath at the board fab, precipitation of copper as hydroxide with lime, or lime neutralisation of downstream acid streams. The ferric-chloride copper etch itself is as sourced.

metal.lime.scavenger.name: Lime as a slag flux in tin, lead and silicon smelting
metal.lime.scavenger.description: Beyond alumina and iron, lime shows up as a cheap flux wherever a siliceous slag has to stay liquid and the impurity has to be dumped: tin smelting adds lime to pull silica and some tungsten into the slag, the lead sinter and blast furnace charge roughly 15-25% limestone, and calcium compounds are added to the silicon furnace feed to mop up alumina. It is the general-purpose garbage collector of the metals industry.

facts.label: Lead sinter
facts.value: order 15-25% limestone in the sinter mix

metal.lime.scavenger.note: Snelter lime practice is very smelter-specific; medium confidence.

metal.lime.slaking.name: Slaking
metal.lime.slaking.description: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, releasing about 65% more mass and enough heat to boil water. Slaking is done in a pan with a rotating rake, or in a ball mill in the paper industry, and the product is a fine white powder or a milk. It is done at the steelworks, at the water treatment plant and at the board fab's causticisation circuit. The safety point that every plant's training programme is about is that a lump of quicklime dropped into a drum of water will split the drum.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, +64% by mass, strongly exothermic

facts.label: Solubility
facts.value: about 1.7 g/L at 20 C - enough to be caustic, not enough to be a base

metal.nickel.sherritt-gordon.name: Sherritt-Gordon ammonia leach and hydrogen reduction
metal.nickel.sherritt-gordon.description: The process that unlocked the laterites in the 1970s and 1980s. The slurry is leached at atmospheric pressure with concentrated ammonia and oxygen at 50-70 C: nickel and copper form soluble ammine complexes while the iron precipitates as hematite. The pregnant liquor is heated in a pressure autoclave with hydrogen and more ammonia, and the nickel comes out of solution as a metal powder while the copper stays in solution as the ammine, so the two separate in one vessel. The powder is filtered, washed and dried in a rotary vacuum dryer. This is genuinely a 1980s technology. The first commercial laterite plant, at Browns River in Queensland, started in 1974 and Sherritt licensed the process to the Cubans and the Japanese in the second half of the decade.

facts.label: Ammonia leach
facts.value: 50-70 C, atmospheric pressure, concentrated NH3, aerated

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: Ni2+ and Cu2+ as [Ni(NH3)6]2+ and [Cu(NH3)4]2+; Fe precipitates as hematite

facts.label: Hydrogen reduction
facts.value: 150-200 C, 20-35 bar H2, in a stirred autoclave

facts.label: Product
facts.value: nickel powder 99%+

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: copper stays in solution and is electrowon separately

facts.label: First commercial plant
facts.value: Browns River, Queensland, 1974

children.name: Ammonia-hydrogen autoclave
children.description: A 10-15 m long, 3-5 m diameter, titanium or 316L-lined pressure vessel in a 6-10 stage cascade. In each stage the liquor is contacted with hydrogen and stirred, and the nickel comes out onto the walls and the cooling surfaces. The whole chemistry depends on the fact that ammonia complexes nickel and copper so strongly that hydrogen alone cannot reduce them at atmospheric pressure; the autoclave gives the extra pressure to push the equilibrium over. Removing the ammonia and boiling the slurry then precipitates basic nickel carbonate, which is calcined to nickel oxide.

facts.label: Vessel
facts.value: 3-5 m diameter, 10-15 m long, 6-10 stages

facts.label: Material
facts.value: carbon steel with titanium or stainless lining

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: a cobalt-nickel or iron-based slurry catalyst seeds the deposition

children.note: Sherritt's own patents cover the details; medium confidence on the vessel dimensions.

metal.silica.czochralski.name: Czochralski monocrystalline ingot
metal.silica.czochralski.description: Where the polysilicon chain ends and the semiconductor business begins. A 2 kg charge is melted at 1414 C in a silica crucible over a seed crystal, and a slow pull at 0.5-2 mm/min with rotation grows a 75-150 mm boule under high-purity argon. Every defect the 6510 die carried (dislocations, oxygen precipitates, the dopant gradient along the length of the ingot) was frozen in during this pull. The ingot is then sawn, lapped and polished into wafers, and the MOS structure is grown and etched on the wafer.

facts.label: Pull rate
facts.value: 0.5-2 mm/min

facts.label: Boule diameter
facts.value: 75-150 mm, yielding 6510 dies of roughly 3-6 mm

facts.label: Ambient
facts.value: high-purity argon over the melt

metal.tin.fluid-bed-reactor.name: Fluid-bed reduction of fine cassiterite (post-1982 route)
metal.tin.fluid-bed-reactor.description: Worth noting as the direction the industry went in rather than as 1982 practice: the fine concentrates that a gravity circuit now produces reduce easily in a fluidised bed at 850-1000 C, which is a temperature no reverberatory furnace can hold at its hearth. This process is why the modern tin industry uses much less coke and produces much less CO. In 1982 essentially none of this existed.

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: lower carbon and lower reductant per tonne; adopted after 1985

metal.tin.fluid-bed-reactor.note: A sibling of the smelting step rather than a stage of it, and dated to later practice: fluid-bed reduction did not exist in the 1982 window, when the reverberatory and electric furnaces were the industry's actual practice.

metal.tin.refining.name: Refine the crude tin to 99.9%
metal.tin.refining.description: Crude tin at 99.5-99.8% still carries iron, copper and arsenic, and the difference between 99.5% and 99.9% matters enormously for solder because iron is a solder poison and raises the liquidus. Two routes. Liquation, the old one, melts the crude tin at about 400 C: tin melts at 232 C, so the iron and copper stay solid and bottom out, and the clean tin is drawn off. Electrolysis, the modern one, uses a stannic chloride or a fluorostannate bath and gives 99.97-99.99%. Malaysia ran electrolysis. Bolivia's low-grade concentrate still used liquation.

facts.label: Liquation
facts.value: melt at 380-400 C; iron and copper stay solid

facts.label: Electrolysis
facts.value: SnCl2/SnCl4 or Na2SnF6 bath; 99.97-99.99% Sn

facts.label: Why it matters
facts.value: iron above ~0.1% wets badly and raises the melting range of solder

metal.tin.smelting.name: Tin smelting
metal.tin.smelting.description: Cassiterite is one of the easiest oxide ores to reduce: SnO2 + C -> Sn + CO2 goes at only 1200-1400 C, far below copper or iron, because tin's oxides are unstable. The Malaysian and Indonesian smelters in 1982 were reverberatory or electric furnaces on 5-20 t capacity, fired with coke, charged with concentrate and about 15% limestone as a flux, and tapped a crude tin at 99.5-99.8% in maybe eight hours. The furnace is a long, narrow, brick-lined box with a step grate at the firebox end, so the charge moves gradually forward and meets rising temperatures. It is a reverberatory used for a purely solid-solid reaction, which is why tin smelting smells of SO2 only when the concentrate is sulphide.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: SnO2 + 2C -> Sn + 2CO; below 1200 C the reduction is too slow

facts.label: Reagent
facts.value: coke or anthracite, 15-25% of concentrate mass

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: 15% limestone, to take silica into the slag

facts.label: Slag
facts.value: iron and silica with some tin left in it - the usual tin smelter loss is 1-3%

metal.tin.smelting.note: Tin smelting is one of the few pyro-metallurgical processes that did not move to electric furnaces until well after 1982.

children.name: Roasting of fluorine-bearing Bolivian concentrate
children.description: Bolivian concentrates carry fluorine, which would carry through into the tin as a stubborn impurity. So they are roasted at 600-800 C before smelting to drive off the fluorine as HF and the arsenic as arsenic oxide, and the hot gas is scrubbed with lime to make calcium fluoride before release. That lime scrub is a genuine environmental control fitted in the 1970s and 1980s, and it is one of the reasons the smelters are the only tin plants with a scrubber.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 600-800 C in a rotary or fluidised-bed roaster

facts.label: Offgas scrub
facts.value: limestone slurry neutralises the HF, giving calcium fluoride

children.note: Applied mainly to Bolivian and Brazilian concentrates; medium confidence on the exact scrub chemistry.

children.name: Dry, sieve and mix the smelter charge
children.description: Cassiterite concentrates are roasted if they carry fluorine or arsenic, dried to remove the 8-12% moisture, and sieved. Because a reverberatory furnace with fine charge in it just makes dust. The charge is then mixed with the limestone flux and the coke, in the ratio that gives 15-20% flux and 15-25% reductant. Nothing about this is clever and everything about it is critical: an Indonesian smelter that got the coke ratio wrong lost a few percent of its tin into the slag, which at 3% is a third of its margin.

facts.label: Moisture in concentrate
facts.value: 8-12%, dried before charging

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: 15-20% limestone

facts.label: Reductant
facts.value: 15-25% coke or anthracite

children.note: Medium confidence; the ratios are typical of Southeast Asian practice.

metal.copper.intrusion.name: Tertiary porphyry intrusion
metal.copper.intrusion.description: A granodiorite or quartz monzonite stock, once liquid and now frozen, with the copper-bearing sulphide veins filling fractures and disseminated grains through it. Under a 100 m of leached, iron-stained capping lies the transition ore and then the primary sulphides, so the pit's first 50-150 m of material is nearly worthless and has to be hauled anyway.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: granodiorite / quartz monzonite porphyry with hydrothermal alteration

facts.label: Oxidation profile
facts.value: leached zone, then mixed sulphide-secondary enrichment, then primary sulphide

metal.caustic-lime-flotation.name: Lime and soda ash as pH regulators
metal.caustic-lime-flotation.description: Flotation needs the ore surfaces clean of slime and the water at a controlled alkaline pH, or the xanthate decomposes to xanthic acid and carbon disulphide and evaporates. Lime from a limestone kiln is the cheapest and most common regulator; soda ash where lime is unavailable; and in the deep concentrators of Chile and Arizona the process water has to be lime-treated hard before use because the Andean water is very soft and very acid.

facts.label: Water treatment
facts.value: lime softening to remove carbonate hardness where process water is soft

metal.caustic-lime-flotation.note: Not established: the 8.0-9.5 pH target, the xanthate-to-xanthic-acid decomposition chemistry, or lime-softening of soft acid process water in Chile and Arizona.

metal.pine-oil-frother.name: Pine oil and MIBC frothers
metal.pine-oil-frother.description: Frothers are oily surfactants that stabilise the air-water interface. Until the 1970s the standard was pine oil distilled from pine stumps and mill residues. It is a forestry residue, not a mineral. Pine oil was being displaced by methyl isobutyl carbinol, a petrochemical, precisely because the natural supply was limited and the synthetic one gave a more stable froth.

facts.label: Pine oil
facts.value: alpha-terpineol-rich fraction, from kraft and sulphite pulp-mill residues

facts.label: Synthetic
facts.value: MIBC (methyl isobutyl carbinol), fully synthetic by the 1980s

metal.pine-oil-frother.note: The pine oil to MIBC transition is well documented in mineral processing literature; medium confidence on exact 1982 split.

metal.xanthate.name: Ethyl xanthate collector
metal.xanthate.description: Xanthate is the workhorse flotation reagent, and it is a petrochemical in disguise: carbon disulphide (from natural gas or from coke-oven gas and methane) reacts with ethanol and caustic soda. Potassium and sodium ethyl xanthates were the standard 1980s collectors for sulphide copper, with a frother on top. So the flotation chemistry that recovers copper in 1982 depends on a sulphur-and-alcohol chain that ends in a gasworks, not a mine.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: CS2 + C2H5OH + KOH -> C2H5OCS2K + H2O

facts.label: Dosage
facts.value: 5-30 g/t of concentrate collector

metal.xanthate.note: Dosage varies with mineralogy and water chemistry; medium confidence on the range.

metal.silica-flux.name: Silica flux from a sand quarry
metal.silica-flux.simple_name: Silica flux from a sand quarry
metal.silica-flux.description: The smelter adds sand or quartzite so that the iron in the concentrate can be thrown off as a slag instead of entering the matte. The quartz is often a cheap nearby dune sand. This is exactly the same material the glass industry buys, and the reason a copper smelter in the 1980s had a sand dryer and a small silica prep plant. The flux is dosed so the slag's silica content matches what the concentrate brings.

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: quartz sand or quartzite, sized 0.1-1 mm

facts.label: Addition
facts.value: order 5-15% of the dry concentrate weight

metal.silica-flux.note: Not established: quartz sand or quartzite as the specific copper-smelter silica flux. General smelting references name limestone or dolomite as the usual flux for removing gangue as slag, and none of them gives a silica dosage of 5-15% of concentrate or the 0.1-1 mm sizing. The claim that the flux is dosed to match the silica the concentrate brings is plausible smelter practice but is not documented in the references fetched.

metal.lime.kiln-gas.name: Lime kiln gas and its CO2
metal.lime.kiln-gas.description: A lime kiln makes carbon dioxide as its main product, roughly 0.44 t of CO2 per tonne of CaO, and in 1982 that gas was usually burnt or dumped because there was nowhere to put it. Its two real uses were the Solvay tower, which is built beside its lime kilns, and (much later) the emerging practice of feeding kiln gas to a nearby chemical plant. So the limestone quarry behind a C64's case carries a hidden carbon footprint that did not become an engineering problem until the 1990s.

facts.label: CO2 yield
facts.value: ~0.44 t of CO2 per tonne of CaO, plus the fuel

facts.label: 1982 fate
facts.value: burnt for heat, or vented; the sequestration era had not arrived

metal.lime.kiln-gas.note: Medium confidence; the stoichiometric yield is certain, the 1982 disposition is a generalisation.

metal.lime.cement.name: Lime in Portland cement
metal.lime.cement.description: By far the largest single use of lime in the world, and the reason the business had a global price: about 90% of all lime produced goes into cement, and cement is the second-largest industrial material after steel. The route is the one already in this branch (limestone, kiln, CaO) and then the clinker: 75-80% limestone with 20-25% clay or shale in a rotary kiln at 1450 C, and the resulting clinker ground with 3-5% gypsum. A C64's case was painted, not cemented, but the cement industry is the reason lime is cheap, and it is a legitimate side door out of this branch.

facts.label: Lime share of lime demand
facts.value: ~90% goes into cement

facts.label: Clinker
facts.value: 75-80% limestone, 20-25% clay, fired at 1450 C in a rotary kiln

facts.label: Gypsum
facts.value: 3-5% added at the cement mill to control the set

metal.nickel.sulphide-concentrate.name: Nickel sulphide concentrate (Sudbury)
metal.nickel.sulphide-concentrate.description: The Sudbury basin of Ontario was the world's nickel capital and it is a genuinely strange deposit: an impact structure full of shock-melted, metal-rich breccia at the base of a 1.8 billion year old impact crater, with pentlandite (Fe,Ni)9S8 and millerite NiS. The INCO operation mined both underground and, from 1962, from the open pit at the south end of the basin, and roasted the ore in fluidised beds to make 'fines' (a nickel-copper matte rather than a concentrate) before smelting. The tree therefore continues down through the Sudbury ore to a shocked sulphide breccia in an impact melt sheet, which is as geologically interesting an endpoint as this tree has.

facts.label: Minerals
facts.value: pentlandite (Fe,Ni)9S8, millerite NiS, pyrrhotite

facts.label: Origin
facts.value: a 1.85 billion year old meteorite impact structure; the ore sits in and below the melt sheet

facts.label: Route
facts.value: fluidised-bed roasting to sinter fines, then smelting to a matte, then converting

metal.nickel.cobalt-carbonyl.name: Dicobalt octacarbonyl, Co2(CO)8
metal.nickel.cobalt-carbonyl.description: The cobalt in a Mond residue is a genuine industrial source, and an unusual one: the residue left after the nickel has been volatilised as Ni(CO)4 still contains the cobalt as Co2(CO)8, and the two carbonyls are separated by exploiting the fact that dicobalt octacarbonyl is solid and will crystallise out while nickel carbonyl boils off at 43 C. In the classical route the residue is treated with copper at about 200 C under hydrogen to reduce both carbonyls, and then re-carbonylated to re-form Co2(CO)8, which is filtered and decomposed to metal. The consequence for the wider market is that every tonne of nickel refined by the carbonyl process is a tonne of cobalt that did not have to be mined, which is why the two nickel carbonyl plants at Sudbury and Kokkola were influential in the cobalt market well beyond their own output.

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: Co2(CO)8 is solid and crystallises; Ni(CO)4 boils at 43 C and distils off

facts.label: Process
facts.value: reduction with copper under hydrogen at about 200 C, then carbonylation, then decomposition to metal

facts.label: Market effect
facts.value: nickel carbonyl plants are a by-product source of cobalt, so nickel capacity sets part of the cobalt supply

metal.nickel.cobalt-carbonyl.note: The chemistry and the plants are well documented. How much cobalt came from this route in 1982 is not established, and the market that year was falling rather than short: about $12.50/lb in May, against $25/lb in 1980 and about $5/lb by 1983-84.

metal.ferronickel.name: Ferronickel, the laterite iron-nickel alloy
metal.ferronickel.description: The dominant way nickel actually became metal in 1982. Dried laterite and quartzite are fed with coke into a large submerged arc furnace, 30-60 MW, three electrodes, running at 1350-1500 C. The laterite's iron is already present as hematite, so the whole charge reduces together and the product is not nickel metal but an alloy of about 60-75% Ni and 25-40% Fe, plus a slag of magnesium, silicon and aluminium oxides. The ferronickel is tapped and either refined in the same operation to pure nickel or (more commonly in the 1980s) sold straight to a stainless steel mill as a charge, which is why the whole ferronickel industry is really a stainless steel industry.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: submerged arc, 30-60 MW, three electrodes, 1350-1500 C

facts.label: Product
facts.value: ferronickel, 60-75% Ni / 25-40% Fe

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 1.5-2.5 t of dried laterite per tonne of Ni in the alloy

facts.label: Charge drying
facts.value: suspension or rotary dryer to reduce the 30-45% moisture of laterite to below 1-2% before the furnace

metal.silica.czochralski.crucible.name: Fused quartz growth crucible
metal.silica.czochralski.crucible.description: The crucible the melt sits in is made from the same silicon chain one step further down, from high-purity quartz fused in vacuum or wet hydrogen to knock out the alkali that would poison a p-type wafer. It is expensive, fragile, and replaced every few hundred pulls.

facts.label: Fusing temperature
facts.value: ~2000 C in vacuum or wet H2

facts.label: Service life
facts.value: a few hundred growth runs in 1980s practice

metal.silica.czochralski.crucible.note: Crucible life varied enormously with melt temperature discipline; treat as order of magnitude.

metal.silica.field-oxide.name: Thermally grown silicon dioxide (SiO2)
metal.silica.field-oxide.description: The gate oxide, the field oxide and the photoresist mask oxide of a 1982 NMOS die are not bought. They are grown out of the silicon itself. A wafer goes into a 1000-1150 C steam or dry-oxygen furnace for an hour and a half and roughly a thousand angstroms of SiO2 comes off the wafer, consuming about 0.1% of its thickness. The machine's entire insulation is therefore chemically the same element as the chip, oxidised in place, and the 6510's gate dielectric is aluminium on oxide rather than a polysilicon gate.

facts.label: Gate oxide
facts.value: ~1000-1500 A in a 1982 NMOS process

facts.label: Wet vs dry
facts.value: dry O2 for the thin gate oxide, wet steam for the thicker field oxide

metal.silica.field-oxide.note: Documented: the silicon dioxide is grown on the wafer rather than deposited (it was first grown accidentally at Bell Labs in 1955) and oxide layer formation is by thermal oxidation or, for the field regions, by local oxidation of silicon (LOCOS). Not established: the 1000-1150 C steam or dry-oxygen furnace, the hour-and-a-half cycle, the roughly 1000-1500 angstrom gate oxide of a 1982 NMOS process, and the 0.1% of wafer thickness consumed.

metal.tin.slag.name: Tin smelter's slag and its tin loss
metal.tin.slag.description: A tin smelter loses 1-3% of its tin into the slag, and the slag is a silicate of iron and silica with tin locked up in it. Recovering that tin is a separate business: the slag is crushed and re-smelted, or in Malaysia and Brazil it was re-smelted in a small furnace to recover the tin. A tin smelter therefore has a second, smaller smelter, and the discipline of a tin plant is judged by its recovery, which is why the industry published recovery figures with a seriousness that most primary metals do not.

facts.label: Loss to slag
facts.value: 1-3% of the tin in the charge

facts.label: Recovery route
facts.value: slag retreatment, historically by resmelting

metal.tin.slag.note: Medium confidence on the loss figure; it varies with the slag basicity and the furnace.

metal.lime.kiln-clinker.name: Overburnt lime and the clinker problem
metal.lime.kiln-clinker.description: If a lime kiln burns a stone too hot for too long, the lime grains sinter together into hard 'clinker' and the lime is unusable: it slakes too slowly and lumps in the mixer. Overburnt lime is a real fraction of the output of a poor kiln and it has to be screened out or ground. The same failure happens in a captive lime kiln feeding a blast furnace, where the operator is watching the furnace's slag chemistry and the lime plant's temperature curve at the same time. It is a small thing and it is a good illustration that lime is a feed, not a commodity.

facts.label: Cause
facts.value: overburning: local temperature above about 1200 C for too long

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: the grains sinter; the lime slakes slowly and lumps in the mixer

metal.lime.kiln-clinker.note: Medium confidence; the mechanism is standard.

metal.nickel.nickel-oxide.name: Nickel oxide (NiO)
metal.nickel.nickel-oxide.description: The commercially traded intermediate. The pregnant solvent is stripped of ammonia and boiled, basic nickel carbonate NiCO3.2Ni(OH)2.4H2O drops out, it is filtered and washed, and it is calcined at 400-600 C to green-black nickel oxide at 99.0-99.5% Ni. In 1982 the overwhelming majority of nickel oxide went to ferronickel smelting. Pure nickel oxide was a smaller but growing market for stainless steel and for plating.
metal.nickel.nickel-oxide.note: The later hydrometallurgical routes (Murrin Murrin, using a sulphate/chloride pressure leach) came after 1982; medium confidence.

metal.nickel.cobalt-catalyst.name: Cobalt-nickel hydrogenation and reduction catalyst (Raney-type)
metal.nickel.cobalt-catalyst.description: A skeletal nickel-cobalt catalyst for hydrogenation and for seeding hydrogen reduction, made by alkali-leaching aluminium from a nickel-aluminium alloy carrying cobalt. Raney nickel itself is nickel from Ni-Al digested with concentrated sodium hydroxide at 70-100 C to a porous sponge of about 100 m2 per gram of nickel surface; cobalt enters as promoter or as co-metal, giving the cobalt-nickel and Raney cobalt variants. In 1982 Grace sold Raney nickel, cobalt and chromium grades for nitro-to-amine, carbonyl-to-alcohol, nitrile-to-amine and olefin/acetylene saturation, and Sherritt-type ammonia-pressure circuits seeded their hydrogen-reduction autoclaves with a cobalt-nickel or iron slurry. The catalyst ships as water-wet slurry, pyrophoric when dry, and is not consumed in the hydrogenation itself.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: Ni-Al with Co promoter, or Co-Al with Ni; Raney cobalt is the cobalt analogue

facts.label: Activation
facts.value: leached with concentrated NaOH at 70-100 C; Al out as aluminate, Ni-Co sponge remains

facts.label: Surface
facts.value: about 100 m2 per gram of nickel for commercial Raney nickel

facts.label: Form
facts.value: water-wet slurry as sold; dry activated powder is pyrophoric

metal.nickel.cobalt-catalyst.note: Established: Raney nickel from Ni-Al leached with NaOH, third-metal promoters, cobalt variants, hydrogenation of benzene to cyclohexane and of nitro/nitrile/olefin groups, Grace Ni/Co/Cr hydrogenation grades, and Sherritt hydrogen under pressure precipitating nickel from ammoniacal solutions. Not established: the exact Co:Ni ratio in any 1982 Sherritt seeding slurry, which refinery bought which grade, or consumption per tonne of nickel. Distinct from the Co-Mo hydrotreating catalyst (sulphur removal, Co2O3 plus MoO3 on alumina) and from the Ni reforming catalyst (Ni on alumina for steam reforming); checked, not duplicates.

metal.nickel.ore.name: Nickel ore, run-of-mine (laterite and sulphide)
metal.nickel.ore.description: Run-of-mine nickel ore at 1-3% Ni, the feed that washing, screening and flotation upgrade to concentrates. Oxide ground is limonite at 0.8-1.5% Ni in goethite and saprolite/silicate at 1.5-3% Ni with green garnierite in serpentinised peridotite; sulphide ground is pentlandite (Fe,Ni)9S8 with pyrrhotite and chalcopyrite at 1-3% Ni in Sudbury-type impact melt and layered intrusions. Ores above about 1.3% Ni are mined, crushed and screened, typically doubling the nickel content before leach or smelt, with sulphide concentrates at 10-20% Ni. In 1982 laterite from Moa, Surigao, New Caledonia and Queensland fed ferronickel and ammonia-leach routes while Sudbury, Thompson and Norilsk sulphide fed matte-converting and Mond-carbonyl refining.

facts.label: Run-of-mine grade
facts.value: 1-3% Ni; mined when above about 1.3% Ni

facts.label: Limonite
facts.value: 0.8-1.5% Ni in goethite (oxide/limonite type)

facts.label: Saprolite/silicate
facts.value: 1.5-3% Ni with garnierite; garnierite pockets run 20-40% Ni

facts.label: Sulphide
facts.value: 1-3% Ni as pentlandite (Fe,Ni)9S8; concentrates at 10-20% Ni

facts.label: Deposit size
facts.value: typically 20 million tonnes and up at about 1% Ni

metal.nickel.ore.note: Established: laterite vs sulphide split, limonite/saprolite grades, garnierite as Ni-Mg silicate in serpentinised peridotite, pentlandite as the dominant sulphide ore, Sudbury impact-melt setting, and the 1.3% mining cut-off with crushing/screening upgrading. Not established: the exact 1982 tonnage split between laterite and sulphide routes, or which mine fed which C64 part. Generic run-of-mine parent noting both types. The specific laterite, sulphide-concentrate, limonite-garnierite and impact-melt nodes remain, not duplicated.

metal.cobalt.liquor.name: Cobalt sulphate liquor
metal.cobalt.liquor.description: Cobalt sulphate pregnant liquor from dissolving cobalt hydroxide or crude metal in sulfuric acid, fed to insoluble anodes and cobalt starter cathodes.
metal.cobalt.liquor.note: Not established: whether 1982 feed was hydroxide, crude metal, or Copperbelt ore leach. Ore anchor is an inferred shortcut.

metal.nickel.carbonate-calcination.name: Nickel carbonate calcination
metal.nickel.carbonate-calcination.description: Ammonia-strip, boil, precipitation and 400-600 C calcination of basic nickel carbonate to 99.0-99.5% NiO for ferronickel, stainless and plating.
metal.nickel.carbonate-calcination.note: Not established: carbonate precipitation detail; post-1982 pressure-leach routes excluded per the oxide note.
